report:
**Conclusion: Yes.** High-quality randomized evidence shows that denosumab (Prolia) reduces *new vertebral fractures* in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis while treatment is maintained.

The pivotal 3-year, placebo-controlled FREEDOM trial found new radiographic vertebral fractures in 2.3% of women receiving denosumab 60 mg every six months versus 7.2% receiving placebo (risk ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.26–0.41; p<0.001). That is a 68% relative reduction and an absolute reduction of 4.9 percentage points (roughly 1 vertebral fracture prevented per 20 women treated for three years, in this trial population). It also reduced hip and nonvertebral fractures.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19671655/

The FDA label independently reports the same trial outcome and states that Prolia significantly reduced new morphometric vertebral fractures at years 1, 2, and 3.  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2011/125320s5s6lbl.pdf

**Important qualification:** this is evidence of benefit *on schedule and during therapy*, not evidence that it can safely be stopped without a plan. In a post-hoc analysis of FREEDOM/FREEDOM Extension participants, vertebral-fracture rates rose after discontinuation to rates seen in untreated participants; multiple vertebral fractures were a particular concern.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29105841/

Denosumab is therefore an effective option, especially for people at high fracture risk, but it is not automatically superior to every alternative: a systematic review/meta-analysis found no statistically significant short-term fracture-risk difference versus bisphosphonates, despite larger bone-density gains with denosumab. Treatment choice and any transition after stopping should be individualized with a clinician.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27120345/
